title: 1 Kings 2:26–35
context: Solomon next deals with Abiathar and with Joab. To Abiathar the priest he says, “Go to Anathoth, to your own fields, for you are worthy of death.” He will not at this time put him to death, because Abiathar bore the Lord GOD’s ark before David and was afflicted in all in which David was afflicted. The narrator then states the theological point in so many words: “So Solomon thrust Abiathar out from being priest to the LORD, that he might fulfill the LORD’s word which he spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.” That fulfillment is shared ground. Both traditions affirm that the earlier word about Eli’s house stands, that it is here carried out in history, and that classical Arminians, no less than Reformed readers, confess God’s exhaustive foreknowledge. The verse does not require a sovereignty fork, and none is drawn. News of these things comes to Joab, who had followed Adonijah though he had not followed Absalom. Joab flees to the LORD’s Tent and holds onto the horns of the altar. Solomon is told, and he sends Benaiah, saying, “Go, fall on him.” Benaiah tells Joab to come out; Joab answers, “No; but I will die here.” Solomon then orders Benaiah to do as Joab has said, to fall on him and bury him, that the blood Joab shed without cause may be taken away from David and from David’s house. The LORD will return that blood on Joab’s head because he fell on Abner the son of Ner and Amasa the son of Jether, two men more righteous and better than he, and David did not know it. Their blood will return on Joab and on his offspring, but for David, his offspring, his house, and his throne there will be peace forever from the LORD. Benaiah goes up, falls on him, and kills him; Joab is buried in his own house in the wilderness. Solomon puts Benaiah over the army in Joab’s place, and Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar. Both traditions report the banishment and the execution as the narrator gives them, without sensationalizing the death at the altar.

verses.text: To Abiathar the priest the king said, “Go to Anathoth, to your own fields, for you are worthy of death. But I will not at this time put you to death, because you bore the Lord GOD’s ark before David my father, and because you were afflicted in all in which my father was afflicted.”
verses.arminianNotes:
To Abiathar the priest the king said, “Go to Anathoth, to your own fields, for you are worthy of death.” He will not at this time put him to death, “because you bore the Lord GOD’s ark before David my father, and because you were afflicted in all in which my father was afflicted.” The sentence is banishment, not execution, and the grounds of sparing are service with the ark and shared affliction. The title “Lord GOD” follows the WEB; a footnote explains “Lord” here as Adonai.

Arminian readers hear a real mitigation. Abiathar is called worthy of death, and he is still sent alive to his fields, for reasons Solomon names from the past.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep both halves: worthiness of death, and a present refusal to put him to death, because of the ark and the shared affliction.

Both traditions describe the banishment as the narrator gives it. Anathoth is named as his own fields; the verse does not require a further geography lesson.

verses.text: So Solomon thrust Abiathar out from being priest to the LORD, that he might fulfill the LORD’s word which he spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.
verses.arminianNotes:
The narrator then interprets the act: “So Solomon thrust Abiathar out from being priest to the LORD, that he might fulfill the LORD’s word which he spoke concerning the house of Eli in Shiloh.” Abiathar’s removal is the fulfillment of that earlier word. The wording of the older prophecy is not quoted here and need not be reconstructed from memory.

Arminian readers take the fulfillment as real history under a God who had spoken beforehand and who knows the end exhaustively. Solomon’s act is the means the narrator names; it does not require a debate about whether foreknowledge is exhaustive, which classical Arminians affirm.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise receive the verse as the book’s own theology of the event. The word spoken concerning Eli’s house at Shiloh is fulfilled when Abiathar is thrust out from being priest to the LORD.

Both traditions treat this prophecy-and-fulfillment as shared ground. The verse does not warrant a sovereignty fork, and none is added.

verses.text: This news came to Joab; for Joab had followed Adonijah, although he didn’t follow Absalom. Joab fled to the LORD’s Tent, and held onto the horns of the altar.
verses.arminianNotes:
“This news came to Joab; for Joab had followed Adonijah, although he didn’t follow Absalom.” Joab flees to the LORD’s Tent and holds onto the horns of the altar. The narrator recalls his earlier choice and shows him seeking the same refuge Adonijah had sought.

Arminian readers hear a man acting on news he has heard. He had followed Adonijah, he had not followed Absalom, and he now takes hold of the altar’s horns by his own decision.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the contrast the verse itself draws. Joab’s past with Adonijah is named, and his flight to the LORD’s Tent is reported without adornment.

Both traditions describe the scene as the text gives it. The Tent and the horns are not turned into a type, and the custom of refuge is not expanded beyond what the narrative shows.

verses.text: King Solomon was told, “Joab has fled to the LORD’s Tent; and behold, he is by the altar.” Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, “Go, fall on him.”
verses.arminianNotes:
King Solomon was told, “Joab has fled to the LORD’s Tent; and behold, he is by the altar.” Then Solomon sent Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, saying, “Go, fall on him.” The king is informed, and the order is given in those words.

Arminian readers hear a deliberate command, not a misunderstanding. Solomon knows Joab is by the altar, and he still says, “Go, fall on him.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same knowledge. The report and the order stand in one verse: Joab is by the altar, and Benaiah is sent to fall on him.

Both traditions report the command plainly. What happens when Benaiah reaches the Tent is told next.

verses.text: Benaiah came to the LORD’s Tent, and said to him, “The king says, ‘Come out!’ ” He said, “No; but I will die here.” Benaiah brought the king word again, saying, “This is what Joab said, and this is how he answered me.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Benaiah came to the LORD’s Tent, and said to him, “The king says, ‘Come out!’ ” He said, “No; but I will die here.” Benaiah brings the king word again of what Joab said and how he answered. The first order meets a refusal; Joab will not come out, and he names the place of his death.

Arminian readers hear a real standoff. Benaiah delivers the king’s word, and Joab freely answers, “No; but I will die here.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep both speeches. “Come out!” is the king’s present word through Benaiah, and Joab’s “No” is his own.

Both traditions let the exchange stand and wait for Solomon’s next instruction. The verse is not dressed up as a scene of spectacle.

verses.text: The king said to him, “Do as he has said, and fall on him, and bury him, that you may take away the blood, which Joab shed without cause, from me and from my father’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king said to him, “Do as he has said, and fall on him, and bury him, that you may take away the blood, which Joab shed without cause, from me and from my father’s house.” Solomon accepts Joab’s word about dying there, and he adds burial and a stated purpose: the blood shed without cause is to be taken away from David’s house. The speech continues in the next verses.

Arminian readers hear a legal and moral claim David’s son now makes. The blood is called groundless, and its removal from the house is the purpose named.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the purpose as Solomon states it. Fall on him, bury him, and take away the blood from me and from my father’s house.

Both traditions report the order as given, without sensationalizing a death at the altar, and they let Solomon’s reason be heard in his own words.

verses.text: The LORD will return his blood on his own head, because he fell on two men more righteous and better than he, and killed them with the sword, and my father David didn’t know it: Abner the son of Ner, captain of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the army of Judah.
verses.arminianNotes:
He continues, “The LORD will return his blood on his own head, because he fell on two men more righteous and better than he, and killed them with the sword, and my father David didn’t know it: Abner the son of Ner, captain of the army of Israel, and Amasa the son of Jether, captain of the army of Judah.” The names and offices are given, and David’s ignorance is stated.

Arminian readers hear a charge already met in David’s last words, now spoken as a return of blood the LORD will accomplish. The two captains are called more righteous and better than Joab, and David is said not to have known the deeds.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same points: the LORD will return the blood, the two men are named and ranked as they are, and David’s lack of knowledge is part of the case.

Both traditions keep the accusation as Solomon states it, matching the charge of verses 5–6, and they do not add details the books have not already supplied.

verses.text: So their blood will return on the head of Joab and on the head of his offspring forever. But for David, for his offspring, for his house, and for his throne, there will be peace forever from the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“So their blood will return on the head of Joab and on the head of his offspring forever. But for David, for his offspring, for his house, and for his throne, there will be peace forever from the LORD.” A source footnote offers seed as an alternative to the word offspring; the verse text follows WEB and reads “offspring”

Arminian readers hear two futures set side by side: blood on Joab’s house, and peace from the LORD for David’s house and throne. The peace is asked and declared as the LORD’s gift, not as a human boast alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the contrast as the close of the speech. Joab’s head and offspring stand under returned blood; David’s offspring, house, and throne are given peace forever from the LORD.

Both traditions receive that close as Solomon’s stated hope and verdict, without turning “forever” into a cue for a separate debate in this verse.

verses.text: Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and fell on him, and killed him; and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then Benaiah the son of Jehoiada went up and fell on him, and killed him; and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.” The act and the burial are told in one sentence. Benaiah goes up, falls on Joab, kills him, and Joab is buried in his own house in the wilderness.

Arminian readers let the narrator’s spare wording stand. The execution is reported, not lingered over, and the burial is in Joab’s own house, in the wilderness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the same restraint. He was killed, and he was buried in his own house in the wilderness.

Both traditions report the death as the narrator gives it, without sensationalizing it and without inventing a fork over succession ethics.

verses.text: The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada in his place over the army; and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The king put Benaiah the son of Jehoiada in his place over the army; and the king put Zadok the priest in the place of Abiathar.” The two offices are reassigned: the army to Benaiah, the priesthood to Zadok, in the places of Joab and Abiathar.

Arminian readers hear a completed settling of the two posts named in this unit. Zadok’s rise matches Abiathar’s removal, and Benaiah takes the command he has just executed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise take the verse as the institutional close of the passage. Army and priesthood are placed in new hands, as the king puts them there.

Both traditions describe the appointments as the text gives them, and they do not press the pairing into a type.
